newsitem.title: CANADA: ELAN CEO says company vulnerable to bid.
newsitem.headline: ELAN CEO says company vulnerable to bid.

text.p: ELAN Energy Inc adopted a poison pill because its board believed the heavy oil producer was vulnerable to a takeover bid, not in response to any specific offer feared in the works, ELAN Chief Executive Verne Johnson said on Tuesday.
"It's just prudent, responsible, board of directors management," Johnson said in a telephone interview.

He said ELAN's disappointing stock market performance, which has hit the company amid difficulties boosting production and a widening price differential between light and heavy crude oil, made it vulnerable to a bid.
Industry attention has turned to intermediate-size heavy oil firms with large land positions as it has become increasingly expensive to develop projects, analysts have said.
Last week, Gulf Canada Resources Ltd launched a C$413 million hostile bid for CS Resources Ltd, which like ELAN, uses high-tech methods to extract the thick crude.

"Heavy oil is rapidly becoming a big boy's game -- either go big or go home type of thing -- because it's very capital intensive and a lot of the capital is up front," Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp, said.
"The fact of the matter is that with CS gone, the microscopes all turn over to ELAN, and certainly shareholders are very unhappy and dispondent."
ELAN shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange were trading at 13.85 in late October and tumbled to as low as 8.95 in May. ELAN on Tuesday was up 0.05 to 9.90 on volume of 228,949 shares.

On the production side, ELAN, whose main operating areas include Cactus Lake in west central Saskatchewan and Lindbergh and Cold Lake in Alberta, had volumes improve in the first quarter after coming in below forecasts in 1996, Johnson said.
But he described the second quarter drilling program so far as "terrible" with the long spring thaw season in western Canada, which also made it difficult to transport production.
Current output is about 34,000 barrels per day, well below expectations, because of shut-in wells, he said.
However, the drilling program for the rest of the year was expected to resume at a busy pace, he said.
"We're quite pleased with our operations. We're certainly being pressured by oil pricing -- base price and differential -- but that's the market," Johnson said.
Before this year, much of ELAN's budget was directed to making extensive use of its single-well steam assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) heavy oil production technology.
But in 1997, spending was redirected to more conventional drilling to bring "proper commercial scale" to projects before implementing more expensive recovery techniques, he said.

Johnson said he was not making public specific forecasts for the company's 1997 production, but said his target was 30-40 percent above 1996, when output averaged 30,300 barrels a day. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
